The email said Income Tax Department in its subject line. Bidisha did not click. She read who had sent it, what it asked for, and the deadline for answering: the twentieth of the month. Her stomach felt tight, but she waited before replying. A colleague, Mohit, had once told her about fake notices, so she opened the official portal by typing its address herself. The same notice sat in her account, with the same date. It was real: her freelance income did not match what a client had reported.

Irfan, who lived in the flat below, had received a similar paper letter in the post. He glanced at the envelope, felt a cold drop in his chest, and slid it into a drawer, hoping it was a mistake. The date came and went. When he finally opened it, a penalty had been added to what was a small difference, and he now needed weeks to sort out something that would have taken an afternoon.

After the matter was settled, Bidisha started a page for side income and a folder for receipts. On the last day of every month she filled both in, so the next filing would have every figure ready.

qa.q: What was the deadline for answering in the notice Bidisha received?
qa.a: It was the twentieth of the month.

qa.q: How did Irfan's handling of his letter differ from Bidisha's handling of the email, and what followed?
qa.a: Bidisha read the details, checked the notice on the official portal and settled it, while Irfan hid his letter in a drawer, missed the date and faced a penalty on a small difference.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he slid the letter into the drawer?
qa.a: Fear, shown by the cold drop in his chest, and a hope that it was a mistake.

qa.q: What could Irfan do now?
qa.a: Irfan could check the official portal, answer what is asked as soon as possible, and ask a qualified tax professional if he is unsure.

grounding: Four approaches to a tax notice: reading it carefully, verifying it on the official portal, ignoring it from fear, and improving record-keeping afterwards.

passage:
In Pranav and Pankaj's house there was one tablet and two boys. A kitchen timer sat beside it: thirty minutes for Pranav, ring, thirty for Pankaj. When the bell went, neither could say the other had played longer, and the old argument stopped before it started.

Two streets over, Hansa got to the remote first one evening, tucked it under a cushion and said, "I was here first." Her little brother Dev complained loudly, their parents came in looking tired, and it stopped being about the cartoon and became about who was in charge.

The next day their father asked them to work out a plan. After a long talk they wrote: Monday, Wednesday and Friday for Hansa; Tuesday, Thursday and the weekend for Dev. Hansa pointed out that Thursday suited Dev's homework better, and that seemed fair to both.

Months later, Hansa's exams came. She noticed she was hardly using her days, and the schedule felt unfair to Dev. She said, "You take my slots for two weeks. We'll even it out after." Dev grinned.

qa.q: How long did each brother get on the tablet?
qa.a: Each brother got thirty minutes.

qa.q: Why did the argument stop for Pranav and Pankaj but turn into a fight for Hansa and Dev, and how did Hansa's family fix it?
qa.a: The timer gave a fixed time so nobody could say the other had played longer, while Hansa hid the remote because she got there first and it became a fight over who was in charge; later Hansa and Dev agreed on days and adjusted them for the exams.

qa.q: What was Dev probably feeling when the remote went under the cushion?
qa.a: Frustrated and unfairly treated, which is why he complained loudly.

qa.q: What could Hansa and Dev do when the exams end?
qa.a: They could talk about the extra time Dev had and agree how it evens out.

grounding: Four approaches to sharing a screen between siblings: a timer, agreed days, grabbing first, and changing the plan when exams come.

passage:
Anjali fixed the date for the Diwali evening on the class calendar, then counted back: rehearsals four weeks before, the hall booked six weeks before, invitations out a month before, and the food order final a week ahead. Every step got a date beside it.

She also listed what the evening would cost, and asked classmates for a small fixed amount each. When the caterer's quote was too high, she priced home-made snacks and found they would cover the difference. A shared sheet tracked every rupee spent.

Uday and Abhinav were in charge of sound and seating. "There's still time," Abhinav said, week after week. On the last afternoon they found the speakers needed a cable nobody had, and thirty chairs were still locked in another room. Parents stood at the doors while the boys ran up and down corridors, and the evening began twenty minutes late.

Then the chief guest's car got stuck in traffic. Anjali leaned to the compere: "Bring the dance forward, swap the order." The audience clapped through the folk dance, and nobody noticed a gap. Afterwards the team wrote in the sheet: next time, leave a buffer between items, and check the sound a week earlier.

qa.q: How late did the evening begin?
qa.a: The evening began twenty minutes late.

qa.q: How did Anjali's early planning differ from what Uday and Abhinav did, and what did each lead to?
qa.a: Anjali gave every step a date and tracked costs, while Uday and Abhinav waited until the last afternoon for sound and seating, so a cable and chairs were missing and the evening began late.

qa.q: What were Uday and Abhinav probably feeling when they found the missing cable and chairs?
qa.a: Panic and embarrassment, since parents were waiting at the doors.

qa.q: What could the team do next year?
qa.a: They could check the sound and seating a week earlier and leave a buffer between items.

grounding: Four approaches to planning a school event: working backward from the date, budget planning, leaving it to the last day, and adapting when the chief guest is late.

passage:
For months Vidya said nothing when her mother-in-law Yamini arrived unannounced, sometimes twice in a week. She smiled, put the kettle on, and cleared her afternoon. Then one evening Yamini said, mildly, "You should use less oil," and Vidya snapped, "Nothing I do is right in this house!" The kitchen went silent. Yamini left early, and Vidya's husband Kunal stared at his plate.

That night Vidya thought about it. Yamini had tried to cook at every visit, even when Vidya had already cooked. Perhaps it was Yamini's way of feeling needed, and Vidya wondered about asking for one special dish each time.

With Kunal, she first settled what they both wanted: a call before visits, and holidays split fairly. Only then did Kunal talk to his parents, saying "we" throughout, and they heard one voice, not two against them.

Diwali was still tense. Afterwards the couple wrote down what helped: Yamini's special dish, the phone calls; and what did not: two big meals in two days. Next year they would host one meal and travel for the other, and stay kinder to everybody.

qa.q: What did Yamini say before Vidya snapped?
qa.a: Yamini said, "You should use less oil."

qa.q: How did Vidya's silence about the visits differ in effect from the couple's joint plan?
qa.a: Her silence let resentment build until a mild comment set off an outburst, while agreeing a shared position first let Kunal speak for both, so his parents heard one voice.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when she snapped?
qa.a: Built-up resentment and hurt, released by a small comment after months of saying nothing.

qa.q: What could Vidya and Kunal do to include Yamini?
qa.a: They could ask Yamini to make one special dish each visit and agree on a call before visits.

grounding: Four approaches to conflict with in-laws: finding the concern behind a demand, agreeing as a couple first, staying silent until an outburst, and reviewing after the festival.

passage:
On the walk home Vinita chanted the seven things for craft class: glue, scissors, red paper, ribbon, beads, a shoe box, old newspaper. She said them over and over, and they stayed with her until her little brother ran up shouting about a dog. By the gate she could only find five.

She took out the class note and read it. Two were missing: ribbon and old newspaper. She folded the note over the list, said each item from memory, peeked, and started again until she could say all seven without a peek. Then she went to bed.

Jagdish knew he forgot things. He told his father, "Ask me tonight what I need for tomorrow's project." At dinner his father did, and Jagdish counted the items off on his fingers.

Seema was sure she would remember four things for the school trip and did not write any down. By evening she recalled only three. She called a classmate to ask, but the phone rang and rang. Seema sat with a crease between her eyebrows, staring at the empty page.

qa.q: What interrupted Vinita's chanting on the walk home?
qa.a: Her little brother ran up shouting about a dog.

qa.q: How did Jagdish's way of remembering differ from Seema's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Jagdish asked his father to quiz him that night and counted the items off on his fingers, while Seema trusted her memory, wrote nothing, and could recall only three of four items and could not reach her classmate.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling with the crease between her eyebrows?
qa.a: Worry and annoyance at herself, since she could not recall the fourth item and nobody answered.

qa.q: What could Seema do now?
qa.a: Seema could ask her teacher or another classmate, and write the list down as soon as she has it.

grounding: Four approaches to remembering a long list: chanting, asking a parent to remind, trusting memory alone, and testing yourself with the list covered.

passage:
Madhav found a brown wallet under the bus seat. He imagined his own father patting empty pockets and going pale. The money in it stopped mattering. He gave the wallet to the conductor and asked him to keep it for the owner.

Irfan found cash in a lane and made a list in his head. Keeping it would buy the cricket bat he wanted. But whoever lost it could be short of money for medicine or the rent. And he would think of it every time he swung the bat. He handed it over at the police post.

Hrithik spotted a crisp hundred-rupee note lying by the kerb, looked left and right, and slipped it into his pocket. Nobody saw. All day his stomach was in a knot. In class he could not look at his friends. Nobody had caught him, but the feeling did.

Kavya found a folded note too and decided to keep it. Her friend Sunita said, "What if whoever lost it doesn't have much?" Kavya thought of the person walking home without it. She turned round and gave the note to the shopkeeper, asking him to look after it.

qa.q: Where did Madhav find the wallet?
qa.a: Madhav found it under the bus seat.

qa.q: How did Hrithik's choice differ from Irfan's and Madhav's, and what did it cost Hrithik?
qa.a: Madhav and Irfan thought of the owner and handed the money in, while Hrithik pocketed the note because nobody saw and felt uneasy all day.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling in class?
qa.a: Guilt and unease, since he could not look at his friends.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do about the note?
qa.a: Hrithik could hand it to a shopkeeper or a teacher to keep for whoever lost it.

grounding: Four ways a child handles found money: imagining the owner's feelings, weighing pros and cons, keeping it because nobody saw, and changing mind after temptation.
